Final Communication Reflection 

Before taking COM 120, I thought communication mainly depended on choosing the right words. This course showed me that communication is also affected by perception, listening, body language, culture, conflict, and relationships. Through class activities and the Japan group project, I learned how to communicate more clearly and become more aware of how others may interpret my behavior. 

Lesson One 

Lesson One introduced the transactional model of communication. Communication is not simply one person sending a message to another. Both people are constantly sending, receiving, and interpreting messages. 

I saw this during the Japan group project. Our group used Microsoft Teams, but replies were sometimes delayed, and responsibilities were unclear at first. Once we divided the presentation into sections, the project became easier. In future group projects, I will suggest roles and deadlines earlier and ask members to confirm decisions. 

Lesson Two 

Lesson Two focused on perception and self-awareness. People can interpret the same behavior differently because of their experiences, culture, and expectations. 

During the Japan project, I learned that silence or indirect answers should not automatically be viewed as rude or dishonest. In Japanese communication, silence may show respect, hesitation, or careful thought. Instead of assuming what someone means, I can use perception checking and ask respectful questions. 

My news analysis also showed me how wording affects perception. AP, Reuters, and Fox News covered the same TikTok issue but used different tones and focused on different details. I learned to compare sources and avoid treating my first interpretation as a fact. 

Lesson Three 

Lesson Three covered verbal communication, nonverbal communication, and listening. Nonverbal communication includes eye contact, posture, facial expressions, tone, gestures, and actions. 

For one activity, I told my mother that I appreciated how she supported me and helped me stay organized. I also helped clean without being asked. This showed me that appreciation can be communicated through both words and actions. 

I also practiced active listening while my mother discussed stress at work. I avoided using my phone, maintained eye contact, asked questions, and paraphrased her feelings. She said she felt heard, but she also noticed that I wanted to give advice too quickly. I learned that listening sometimes means supporting someone instead of immediately trying to fix the problem. 

Lesson Five 

Lesson Five taught me about intercultural communication. Culture can affect directness, eye contact, gestures, silence, and expectations about respectful behavior. 

While researching Japan, I learned that American communication habits should not be treated as the standard for everyone. Strong eye contact and direct disagreement may be accepted in American situations but may create discomfort in a formal Japanese interaction. 

My plan for improving intercultural communication is to slow down before judging unfamiliar behavior. I will pay attention to the situation, ask respectful questions, and remember that cultural patterns do not describe every individual. 

Lesson Six 

Lesson Six focused on assertive communication and conflict. Assertive communication means expressing feelings and needs clearly without attacking the other person. 

I practiced this with my mother because she sometimes reminds me several times about the same chore. I told her, “I feel frustrated when I am reminded several times about the same chore because I feel like I am not trusted to handle my responsibilities.” 

She explained that she repeated herself because she worried I would forget. We agreed that she would remind me once, and I would complete the chore or tell her when I planned to do it. I also agreed to set a reminder on my phone. This showed me that assertive communication can solve problems while respecting both people. 

Lesson Seven 

Lesson Seven showed me that relationships and groups require communication, support, appreciation, and clear expectations. 

The activities with my mother taught me not to assume that people already know I appreciate them. Expressing appreciation and listening to her concerns helped improve our relationship. 

The Japan project also showed me that groups need clear responsibilities. At first, the project felt disorganized, but dividing the work helped everyone contribute. During future group projects, I will suggest a shared document, assign sections earlier, and create a deadline before the final due date. 

Conclusion 

COM 120 helped me understand that effective communication requires more than speaking clearly. It also requires listening, checking perceptions, noticing nonverbal behavior, respecting cultural differences, and handling conflict assertively. My main goals are to speak up earlier, avoid making quick assumptions, and listen before offering advice. These skills will help me communicate more effectively in academic, personal, and professional situations.
